parts.name: Engine, small pump
parts.desc: 100 kN turbopump. Chamber, nozzle and cycle are yours to choose.
parts.role: A small engine, 100 kN: an upper-stage or lander class, or one of many in a cluster.
parts.detail: The small turbopump moves enough propellant for 100 kN of thrust: fine for a tiny ship or an upper stage, not enough to lift a crewed vehicle alone. Under a cluster thrust structure every mount gets one, so nine of them push like one large engine. Choose the chamber (fuel), the nozzle, the pump cycle and the igniter.
cons: 100 kN: less than the weight of any crewed ship
Per kilonewton, the dearest and heaviest pump
parts.real: RL10 / Rutherford class

parts.name: Engine, medium pump
parts.desc: 300 kN turbopump. Chamber, nozzle and cycle are yours to choose.
parts.role: A medium engine, 300 kN, alone or in a cluster.
parts.detail: The medium turbopump: 300 kN of thrust and a reasonable price. One lifts about 25 tonnes with a healthy margin; three, five or seven under a cluster thrust structure lift a full crewed ship. Choose the chamber (fuel), the nozzle, the pump cycle and the igniter.
cons: Lifts about 25 t alone, no more
parts.real: RD-0124 / Vinci class

parts.name: Engine, large pump
parts.desc: 1,000 kN turbopump. Runs hot at full throttle.
parts.role: A large engine, 1,000 kN. Runs hot at full throttle.
parts.detail: The large turbopump moves almost 300 kg of propellant a second: a megawatt-class machine. It can lift a big single-stage ship on its own, and it overheats fastest at full throttle. Per kilonewton it is the cheapest and lightest pump, which is why most shapes use one big engine instead of many small ones.
pros: 1,000 kN: about the weight of 100 t
parts.real: Merlin 1D / Vulcain class

parts.name: Single-engine thrust frame, small
parts.desc: A short skirt and thrust cone for one engine under a slim stack.
parts.role: Carries the thrust of one engine into a narrow (small-diameter) stack.
parts.detail: The same idea as the medium single-engine frame, sized for a 1.9 m stack: a skirt on top, and inside it a cone of beams that gathers the push of the engine at one gimbal point and spreads it into the tank wall. Under a wider body the game adds a conical adapter.
cons: One engine: if it fails, the flight is over
Narrow: under a wide body the game adds an adapter
parts.real: Redstone / Mercury-Redstone tail unit (one A-7, 350 kN, 1.78 m wide)

parts.name: Single-engine thrust frame
parts.desc: A skirt and a cone of beams that carry one big engine.
parts.role: The structure that takes the thrust of one engine and spreads it into the tank walls.
parts.detail: Every engine pushes on something. The thrust frame is a cone of beams and stringers between the engine mount and the bottom of the tank: it carries the whole thrust of the engine into the stage, and holds the gimbal actuators, the feed lines and the fins. One engine is the simplest tail there is.
cons: One engine: if it fails, the flight is over
parts.real: Delta II first-stage thrust section (one RS-27A, 890 kN at sea level)

parts.name: Single-engine thrust frame, wide
parts.desc: A wide 4.6 m frame for one engine and a pair of big boosters.
parts.role: Carries one engine under a wide core and gives big strap-on boosters a strong place to push.
parts.detail: A wide core stage with one main engine: the frame is a deep cone of beams under a broad skirt. Its rim is stiff enough to take the thrust of two big solid boosters, which is how Ariane 5 flew: the solids did 90 % of the lifting at liftoff and the one Vulcain engine ran all the way to orbit. Under a narrower body the game adds a flared adapter.
pros: Room for a large engine and its plumbing
parts.real: Ariane 5 core stage engine bay (one Vulcain 2, 1,359 kN in vacuum, 5.4 m wide)

parts.name: Boattail skirt
parts.desc: A tapered aerodynamic skirt that wraps the top of one engine.
parts.role: A thrust frame inside a tapering skirt that shields the engine's plumbing from the airflow.
parts.detail: The boattail is the tapering skirt at the very bottom of a stage. Inside it the thrust frame holds the engine; the skirt itself wraps the turbopump and feed lines, so the rushing air and the heat of the exhaust do not reach them, and the air slides off the base with less drag. Atlas V hides the top of its RD-180 in one; the skirt also stiffens the tail where the solid boosters push.
parts.real: Atlas V boattail (one RD-180, 3,830 kN at sea level, 3.8 m core)

parts.name: Twin-engine thrust frame
parts.desc: Two engines side by side on one cross-beam.
parts.role: A frame for two engines side by side: twice the thrust of one, no engine-out.
parts.detail: A heavy cross-beam spans the bottom of the stage with an engine hanging from each end. Two engines lift twice what one does, for the price of a second engine and a heavier frame. Losing either engine still ends the flight, and the stack must steer against twice the twisting force if one gimbal fails. Titan II flew two chambers like this, and the core of India’s LVM3 flies two Vikas engines.
pros: Twice the thrust of one engine
cons: No engine-out: either failure ends the flight
parts.real: Titan II (LR87, two chambers, 1,913 kN at sea level) · LVM3 L110 core (two Vikas, 766 kN each, 4 m)

parts.name: Three-engine thrust frame
parts.desc: Three engines in a triangle: the Space Shuttle's tail.
parts.role: A frame for three engines in a triangle. It can lose one and still fly.
parts.detail: The Space Shuttle's aft fuselage carried three main engines in a triangle, one on top and two below. A huge truss of titanium and boron-epoxy struts took their 5.6 MN into the orbiter. With three engines a failure is survivable: on STS-51-F one engine shut down early and Challenger still reached orbit on the other two.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
parts.real: Space Shuttle aft fuselage (three RS-25, 1,860 kN each at sea level)

parts.name: Four-engine thrust frame
parts.desc: Four chambers in a square, as under the Soyuz core and Ariane 4.
parts.role: A frame for four engines in a square. Each chamber counts as one engine here.
parts.detail: Korolev's answer to combustion instability was to use four smaller chambers instead of one huge one: the Soyuz core engine RD-108 has four chambers in a square, fed by one turbopump. Ariane 4 and the Long March 2 fly four separate engines the same way. Here each chamber counts as one engine. A failure still ends the flight.
pros: Four small chambers are easy to make burn smoothly
parts.real: Soyuz core (RD-108A: four chambers, 792 kN at sea level) · Ariane 4 (four Viking 5C)

parts.name: Five-engine thrust structure
parts.desc: Four engines in a square around a fifth: the Saturn V first stage.
parts.role: A big frame for five engines: four steering engines at the corners, one fixed in the middle.
parts.detail: The Saturn V's first stage (S-IC) carried five F-1 engines on a thrust structure of crossed beams and four thrust posts. The centre engine was bolted straight; the four outer ones swivelled to steer and stuck out past the edge of the stage, each under a fairing with a fin. Together they made 34.5 MN, still the most powerful single-chamber engines ever flown. It could lose an engine late in the burn and still reach orbit.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
Wide stance for big boosters and fins
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC thrust structure (five F-1, 6,770 kN each, 10.1 m wide)

parts.name: Seven-engine thrust structure
parts.desc: Six engines in a ring around a seventh: New Glenn's tail.
parts.role: A frame for seven engines in a hexagon. It can lose one and still fly.
parts.detail: Seven engines pack into a circle with no gaps: one in the middle, six around it. Blue Origin's New Glenn flies seven BE-4 methane engines this way under a 7 m booster that lands on six legs. Seven medium engines push like two large ones and survive the loss of one.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
parts.real: New Glenn first stage (seven BE-4, 17,100 kN at liftoff, 7 m wide)

parts.name: Octaweb (9 engines)
parts.desc: Eight engines in a ring around a ninth: the Falcon 9 tail.
parts.role: A frame for nine engines: one in the middle, eight around it.
parts.detail: SpaceX's Octaweb holds nine Merlin engines: eight in a circle and one in the centre, under a base heat shield. Nine small engines are cheaper to build in series than one big one, and the rocket can lose one and still reach orbit (engine-out capability). All nine are the same engine: choose it below. Nine small pumps cost about as much as two large engines and push like one.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
Fine thrust steps: nine small or nine medium
cons: Nine engines to buy and plumb
Heavier frame than a single engine
parts.real: Falcon 9 Octaweb (nine Merlin 1D, 7,607 kN at liftoff) · Electron (nine Rutherford)

parts.name: Atlas booster section (3 engines)
parts.desc: A skirt with two bulging engine fairings for the booster engines and a sustainer between them: the stage-and-a-half Atlas.
parts.role: Three engines in a row: two booster engines in side fairings and a sustainer in the middle.
parts.detail: Atlas was a 'stage and a half': every engine lit on the pad, then after about two minutes the whole skirt with the two outer booster engines slid off the back, and the sustainer in the middle burned on alone. Its stainless-steel balloon tanks were so thin they had to stay pressurised or fold under their own weight. In this hangar nothing drops off, and all three engines are the same type, although the real sustainer was much smaller than the boosters.
pros: All engines start on the pad, none in flight
Wide stance for the outer engines
cons: No engine-out: every engine must work
parts.real: Mercury-Atlas LV-3B (1960–63): two XLR89-5 booster engines (1,517 kN together) in a jettisoned skirt 4.9 m across its fairings, one XLR105-5 sustainer (363 kN), two LR101 verniers; 3.0 m stainless-steel balloon tanks

parts.name: Twin-engine thrust frame, wide
parts.desc: Two engines side by side under a wide core: Vulcan, H3, Long March 5.
parts.role: A wide frame for two engines, with a strong rim for big boosters.
parts.detail: Many heavy rockets put two engines under a wide core and clamp big boosters round it: the core burns for minutes, the boosters for the first two. A beam frame spans the base with an engine hanging from each side, and the rim carries the boosters' push into the core. Two engines give twice one engine's thrust, but losing either still ends the flight.
pros: Room for two big engines and their plumbing
cons: Heavier than the medium twin frame
parts.real: Vulcan (two BE-4, 5.4 m) · H3 first stage (two LE-9, 1,471 kN each, 5.27 m) · Long March 5 core (two YF-77, 700 kN vacuum each, 5 m)

parts.name: Three-engine thrust frame, wide
parts.desc: Three engines in a triangle under a wide stack: the Space Shuttle at full width.
parts.role: A wide frame for three engines in a triangle. It can lose one and still fly.
parts.detail: The Space Shuttle’s aft fuselage carried three main engines in a triangle, one on top and two below, beside an external tank 8.4 m wide. A truss of titanium and boron-epoxy struts took their push into the orbiter. With three engines a failure is survivable: on STS-51-F one engine shut down early and Challenger still reached orbit on the other two.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
Room for big boosters at the sides
cons: Heavier than the medium three-engine frame
parts.real: Space Shuttle aft fuselage (1981–2011): three RS-25, 1,860 kN each at sea level; external tank 8.4 m wide

parts.name: Eight-engine thrust structure
parts.desc: Four steering engines round four fixed ones: the Saturn I and IB first stage.
parts.role: A frame for eight engines in two squares.
parts.detail: The Saturn IB's first stage clustered eight H-1 engines: four fixed in an inner square, canted 3° out, and four outer ones canted 6° that swivelled to steer, with eight fins round the tail. Its tanks were a cluster too: eight Redstone-sized tanks round one Jupiter-sized tank.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
Eight engines spread the heat and the load
parts.real: Saturn IB S-IB (1966–75): eight H-1, 7,100 kN total, 6.53 m wide, eight fins spanning 12.0 m; inner engines on a 32 in radius canted 3°, outer on a 95 in radius canted 6° and gimballed (Saturn I documents)

parts.name: Five-engine thrust cone
parts.desc: Five engines in a cross on a cone of beams: the Saturn V second stage.
parts.role: A light frame for five engines made for thin air.
parts.detail: The S-II carried five J-2 hydrogen engines on a conical thrust structure under its huge hydrogen tank, the centre engine fixed and the four outer ones swivelling to steer. It lit about 67 km up, so it needed no fins and its engines wear long bells made for near-vacuum. On Apollo 13 heavy shaking (POGO) shut the centre engine down two minutes early and the outer four burned longer to make up for it.
pros: Can lose one engine and fly on
parts.real: Saturn V S-II (1967–73): five J-2, 4,400 kN in vacuum, Isp 421 s, 10 m wide, centre engine fixed and four gimballed

parts.name: Engine section with boattail (4 engines)
parts.desc: Four hydrogen engines in a square inside a tapering boattail: the SLS core stage.
parts.role: A deep engine section for four engines, with a boattail that shields their tops.
parts.detail: The base of the SLS core stage is its most complex part: a thrust structure for four RS-25 engines with their hydraulic steering on top, wrapped in a boattail that tapers in towards the bells. The engines are veterans of Space Shuttle flights. The two big solid boosters push on the core through its forward and aft attach points.
pros: Shields the engine plumbing from air and heat
parts.real: SLS core stage engine section and boattail (2022–): four RS-25, about 7,440 kN at liftoff, about a fifth of the 39.1 MN of the whole rocket, 8.4 m wide

parts.name: Super Heavy engine bay (33 engines)
parts.desc: Thirty-three engines in three rings under a 9 m steel booster: Super Heavy.
parts.role: A frame for 33 engines: the inner 13 swivel to steer, the outer 20 are fixed.
parts.detail: SpaceX's Super Heavy carries 33 Raptor engines: three in the centre, ten round them and twenty round the edge. The inner thirteen swivel on electric actuators and relight to land; the outer twenty only push at launch. There are no landing legs: the booster flies back to the launch tower, which catches it with two arms.
pros: Can lose engines and fly on
The most thrust of any stage
cons: Thirty-three engines to buy and plumb
parts.real: Super Heavy (2023–): 33 Raptor, 73.5 MN (Block 1) to 80.8 MN (Block 3) at liftoff, 9 m wide, 13 engines with electric thrust vectoring, caught by the tower since 13 October 2024

parts.name: Starship engine bay (6 engines)
parts.desc: Three steering engines in the middle and three fixed vacuum engines round them: Starship.
parts.role: A frame for six engines in two triangles, each in its own shielded bay.
parts.detail: Starship's three sea-level Raptors sit on a thrust puck at the bottom of the oxygen tank, braced by a steel cone, and swivel to steer and land. The three vacuum Raptors, with much bigger bells, are bolted fixed to the aft dome round them. Each engine sits in its own shielded compartment. In this hangar all six take the same engine.
pros: Three swivelling engines steer and land
Each engine in its own shielded bay
cons: In this hangar all six share one nozzle type
parts.real: Starship upper stage (2023–): three Raptor (sea level, gimballed; electric actuators since flight test 2) and three Raptor Vacuum, 9 m wide; Block 4 to add three more vacuum engines

parts.name: Carbon thrust structure (9 engines)
parts.desc: Nine small engines under a slim carbon-fibre stage: Rocket Lab's Electron.
parts.role: A light frame for nine small engines on a narrow stack.
parts.detail: Electron is built almost entirely of carbon composite. Its nine Rutherford engines have pumps spun by electric motors running on lithium-polymer batteries, and almost every engine part is 3D printed. A small rocket, 1.2 m wide and 18 m tall, made for small satellites; Rocket Lab has also fished first stages out of the sea after parachute splashdowns.
pros: Nine small engines: cheap to build in series
cons: Narrow: a wide body needs an adapter
parts.real: Electron first stage (2017–): nine Rutherford, 224 kN sea level / 234 kN vacuum, Isp 311 s, 1.2 m wide, carbon composite

parts.name: Six-engine ring (Proton)
parts.desc: Six engines in a ring, one under each of six outer fuel tanks: Proton.
parts.role: A ring of six engines with an empty centre.
parts.detail: Proton's first stage is a central oxidiser tank ringed by six fuel tanks, each with one RD-275M engine underneath. Each engine swivels sideways in one plane, and together they steer the rocket in every direction. The tail looks like six rockets bundled round a seventh. Kerosene and oxygen stand in for its propellants here.
pros: Engines at the rim steer strongly
parts.real: Proton-M first stage (2001–): six RD-275M (N₂O₄/UDMH), 10,532 kN, Isp 285 s, 4.1 m oxidiser tank, 7.4 m across the fuel tanks, each engine swivels about 7° in one plane

parts.name: Thirty-engine ring (N1)
parts.desc: Twenty-four fixed engines round the rim and six inside, under a wide cone: the Soviet N1.
parts.role: A huge cone of thirty fixed engines that steers by throttling them.
parts.detail: The N1’s first stage carried 30 NK-15 engines: 24 round its 17 m base and six inside at about half that width. None swivelled: the flight control system pitched and yawed the rocket by throttling engines on opposite sides of the outer ring, and the KORD system shut down any engine that failed together with the one opposite. All four launches, from 1969 to 1972, failed in the first stage: a fire and false shutdowns, a turbopump that exploded on the pad, a roll the controls could not stop, and a pressure surge when the inner six shut down. Its engines, improved as the NK-33, later flew on Antares and Soyuz-2.1v.
pros: Steers itself by throttling: no gimbals
Built to lose engines and fly on
cons: Thirty engines to buy and plumb
parts.real: N1 Block A (1969–72): 30 NK-15, 45,400 kN, 17 m base, inner six at about half the diameter, four lattice fins, pitch and yaw by differential throttling of the outer 24, KORD engine shutdown in opposite pairs

parts.name: Hydrogen core frame (4 engines)
parts.desc: Four hydrogen engines in a square under a wide core, with hard points for four boosters: Energia.
parts.role: A wide frame for four engines in a square and four big boosters.
parts.detail: Energia's core stage burned hydrogen in four RD-0120 engines while four kerosene boosters did most of the lifting. Its payload rode on the side of the core instead of on top: the Polyus battle station in 1987 and the Buran shuttle in 1988. Both launches worked; Polyus was lost after separation by a fault of its own.
pros: Four engines in a square: simple and strong
Hard points for four big boosters
parts.real: Energia Block Ts core (1987–88): four RD-0120 (1,526 kN sea level / 1,961 kN vacuum each, Isp 354 / 455 s), 7.75 m wide

parts.name: Strap-on solid motor
parts.desc: A thrust-augmentation solid: 480 kN in vacuum (about 430 kN at sea level) for 47 s, then dead weight.
parts.role: A solid motor clamped to the side: huge thrust at liftoff, for the money.
parts.detail: A tube of wound graphite fibre packed with solid propellant (ammonium perchlorate, aluminium powder, rubber binder). Light it and it burns to the end: no throttle, no shutdown. Delta II flew with three, four or nine of these. They are the cheapest thrust there is for the first minute, but in this hangar nothing separates in flight, so the empty casing rides along as dead mass. Rockets fly them in evenly spaced sets.
pros: About 430 kN off the pad for $320k
cons: Empty casing stays attached (no staging yet)
parts.real: GEM-40 (Delta II): 644 kN, Isp 274 s, 11.8 t propellant, 63 s, 11 m × 1.0 m

parts.name: Large strap-on solid
parts.desc: 800 kN in vacuum (about 720 kN at sea level) for 47 s. The Atlas V / Vulcan class strap-on.
parts.role: A bigger solid motor: about 720 kN off the pad for a heavy stack.
parts.detail: The large graphite-epoxy strap-on, with a canted nozzle so its thrust passes near the centre of the stack. Each one adds about 720 kN off the pad (800 kN in vacuum) and fourteen tonnes of propellant. Two of them lift a stack the main engine alone could never move. The burned-out casing stays attached in this hangar, so each costs Δv later.
pros: About 720 kN off the pad each
cons: Empty casing stays attached (no staging yet)
parts.real: GEM-63 (Atlas V since 2020): 1,650 kN, Isp 279 s, 44 t propellant, 98 s · GEM-63XL (Vulcan): 2,060 kN

parts.name: Segmented solid booster
parts.desc: A Shuttle-type booster in four steel segments: 1,200 kN in vacuum (about 1,090 kN at sea level) for 58 s.
parts.role: The biggest booster: two of them lift a heavy stack off the pad almost alone.
parts.detail: A steel case built from segments, each cast full of propellant and joined at the launch site with pinned field joints sealed by rubber O-rings. The nozzle swivels to steer. Two of these did 70 % of the Shuttle's lifting at liftoff, and Ariane 5 flew on two of its own. Here it is scaled down to fit the ship.
pros: About 1,090 kN off the pad each
Cheapest thrust per kilonewton of any booster
cons: 3.2 t casing stays attached (no staging yet)
parts.real: Space Shuttle SRB: 12,000 kN at liftoff, Isp 242 / 268 s, 500 t propellant, 123 s, 45.5 m × 3.7 m · Ariane 5 P241: 7,080 kN, 240 t, 130 s

parts.name: Liquid strap-on booster
parts.desc: A kerosene booster with its own engine: 450 kN in vacuum (about 390 kN at sea level) for 80 s, Isp 305 s.
parts.role: A whole small rocket clamped to the side: better Isp than a solid, at a solid's price.
parts.detail: Each booster is a cone-topped pair of tanks with its own four-chamber kerosene engine and two steering verniers. Four of them around a core make the Korolev cross: the R-7 cross that launched Gagarin and every Soyuz since. Liquid boosters waste less propellant than solids (higher Isp), but they are heavier for their thrust because they carry tanks, pumps and plumbing. Their empty shells stay attached in this hangar.
pros: Isp 305 s: far better than a solid
Proven: the R-7 family has flown more than 1,900 times
cons: Dearer than a solid of the same thrust
Heavier than a solid for the same thrust
Empty shell stays attached (no staging yet)
parts.real: Soyuz boosters (Blocks B, V, G, D): RD-107A, 839 kN at sea level / 1,020 kN vacuum, Isp 263 / 320 s, about 39 t propellant, 118 s, 19.6 m × 2.7 m

parts.name: Five-segment solid booster
parts.desc: The SLS booster: a Shuttle booster with a fifth segment, 1,440 kN in vacuum (about 1,310 kN at sea level) for 61 s.
parts.role: The biggest solid booster ever flown: longer, stronger, and thrown away after one flight.
parts.detail: Northrop Grumman added a fifth segment to the Space Shuttle's booster. Each of the two on SLS gives about 14.6 MN at liftoff for about two minutes, the largest solid motors ever flown; together they give about four fifths of the thrust at liftoff. Unlike the Shuttle's boosters they are not fished out of the sea and reused.
pros: About 1,310 kN off the pad each
parts.real: SLS five-segment booster (2022–): 14,600 kN max at sea level, Isp 268 s, about 640 t propellant, 126 s, 54 m × 3.71 m, steel segments, not recovered

parts.name: Titan solid booster
parts.desc: A five-segment, 3 m solid with a tank of nitrogen tetroxide strapped along its side for steering: Titan III. 970 kN in vacuum (about 880 kN at sea level) for 58 s.
parts.role: A big solid that steers without moving its nozzle.
parts.detail: The Titan III's two boosters lit on the pad and did all the lifting for nearly two minutes; the core engines only lit seconds before the boosters fell away. The nozzles were fixed: to steer, valves injected nitrogen tetroxide from the tank on the side into one side of the exhaust, bending the jet. Titan IIIE rockets launched both Vikings to Mars and both Voyagers.
pros: About 880 kN off the pad each
cons: 3 t casing and the injectant tank stay attached
parts.real: UA1205 (Titan IIIC, IIID, IIIE; first flight 1965): five segments, 120 in (3.05 m) × 85 ft (25.9 m), about 5,300 kN each, Isp 263 s, about 115 s; liquid-injection thrust vector control with an external N₂O₄ nacelle

parts.name: Carbon-cased solid booster
parts.desc: A one-piece carbon-fibre solid: 930 kN in vacuum (about 840 kN at sea level) for 65 s. Ariane 6 and Vega C.
parts.role: A stubby, light booster wound from carbon fibre in one piece.
parts.detail: The P120C is the largest one-piece carbon-fibre solid motor ever built: 3.4 m wide and 13.5 m long, holding about 142 tonnes of propellant. The same motor is the first stage of Vega C and, two or four at a time, the booster of Ariane 6. Its nozzle tilts on a flexible pivot, pushed by electric actuators instead of hydraulics.
parts.real: P120C (2022–): 4,500 kN average / 4,780 kN max, Isp 280 s, about 142 t propellant, 134 s, 3.4 m × 13.5 m, filament-wound carbon-fibre case, flexible-pivot nozzle with electromechanical actuators

parts.name: SRB-3 solid booster
parts.desc: Japan's H3 booster: 755 kN in vacuum (about 680 kN at sea level) for 55 s, fixed nozzle.
parts.role: A simple solid with a fixed nozzle; the core engines steer.
parts.detail: The H3’s SRB-3 is 2.5 m wide and 15 m long, with a carbon-fibre case. To cut cost its nozzle is fixed, unlike the swivelling nozzle of the older H-IIA booster, so the core engines do all the steering, and it lets go of the core with a simpler separation system. H3 flies with none, two or four of them.
pros: About 680 kN off the pad each
parts.real: SRB-3 (2023–): 2,300 kN max, Isp 283.6 s, 110 s, 15 m × 2.5 m, 76.2 t gross, carbon-fibre case, fixed nozzle, simplified separation

parts.name: S200 solid booster
parts.desc: India's big segmented solid with a swivelling flex nozzle: 970 kN in vacuum (about 870 kN at sea level) for 64 s. LVM3.
parts.role: A huge solid that lifts and steers LVM3 alone for its first two minutes.
parts.detail: Each S200 holds about 205 tonnes of HTPB-based propellant in a 3.2 m case 25 m long. Its flexible nozzle swivels up to 8° on electro-hydraulic actuators, so the boosters steer while the core engines wait: LVM3's core only lights about 110 s after liftoff. LVM3 launched Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023.
pros: About 870 kN off the pad each
parts.real: S200 (LVM3, 2014–): three segments, peak 5,150 kN, average 3,578 kN, Isp 274.5 s, about 205 t HTPB propellant, about 128–130 s, 25 m × 3.2 m, flex nozzle ±8° on 294 kN electro-hydraulic actuators

parts.name: Hydrogen strap-on core
parts.desc: A whole hydrogen first stage with its own RS-68, clamped to the side: 850 kN in vacuum (about 740 kN at sea level) for 80 s.
parts.role: A liquid booster as wide as the core: Delta IV Heavy's side cores.
parts.detail: Delta IV Heavy was three identical Common Booster Cores side by side, each with one RS-68 (the uprated RS-68A from 2012), the most powerful hydrogen engines ever flown. All three lit together; the centre one throttled back to save propellant and burned on after the side cores dropped away. The RS-68 has an ablative nozzle and about 80 % fewer parts than the Shuttle’s engine, at about 10 % less Isp.
pros: Isp 360 s at sea level: far better than a solid
Hydrogen: the highest Isp of any booster here
parts.real: Delta IV Heavy Common Booster Core (2004–24): one RS-68 (2004–11) or RS-68A (from 2012; 3,137 kN sea level / 3,560 kN vacuum, Isp 360 / 412 s), about 200 t propellant, 40.8 m × 5.1 m, ablative nozzle

parts.name: Falcon 9 side booster
parts.desc: A whole Falcon 9 first stage with nine engines, grid fins, legs and a nose cone: 1,075 kN in vacuum (about 975 kN at sea level) for 77 s.
parts.role: A reusable kerosene booster with its own nine engines.
parts.detail: Falcon Heavy is three Falcon 9 first stages side by side: 27 Merlin engines and 22.8 MN at liftoff. The side boosters carry nose cones instead of an upper stage. After separation they turn round, fly back and land side by side near the launch site. In this hangar nothing separates, so they ride all the way.
pros: Isp 282 s at sea level: far better than a solid
Burns the same kerosene and oxygen as the core
cons: Empty shell, legs and grid fins stay attached
parts.real: Falcon Heavy side booster (2018–): nine Merlin 1D, about 7,600 kN sea level, Isp 282 / 311 s, 3.7 m wide, nose cone, titanium grid fins, four legs; 14 Falcon Heavy flights to October 2026

parts.name: Energia Blok A booster
parts.desc: A kerosene booster with a four-chamber RD-170, the most powerful liquid engine ever flown: 1,050 kN in vacuum (about 960 kN at sea level) for 78 s.
parts.role: A huge liquid booster; the same stage became Zenit's first stage.
parts.detail: Each of Energia's four Blok A boosters carried one RD-170: four chambers fed by a single 170-megawatt turbopump, burning kerosene in an oxygen-rich staged-combustion cycle, made to be reused up to ten times. Zenit flew the same stage as its first stage, and the two-chamber RD-180 cut from the same design powered Atlas V.
parts.real: Energia Blok A (1987–88): one RD-170, 7,250 kN sea level / 7,900 kN vacuum, Isp 309 / 338 s, 156 s, 39.5 m × 3.92 m, about 340 t fuelled

parts.name: Angara URM-1 booster
parts.desc: A standard kerosene module with one RD-191: 700 kN in vacuum (about 645 kN at sea level) for 80 s.
parts.role: A building-block booster: Angara makes every size of rocket from the same module.
parts.detail: Angara is a family built from one Universal Rocket Module, URM-1, with a single RD-191: a one-chamber engine cut from the four-chamber RD-170, which throttles from 27 to 105 %. Angara 1.2 flies one module; Angara A5 clusters five, a core and four boosters.
parts.real: Angara URM-1 (2014–): one RD-191, 1,920 kN sea level / 2,090 kN vacuum, Isp 310.7 / 337 s, throttle 27–105 %, about 2.9 m wide, the same module as the core

parts.name: Long March 5 booster
parts.desc: A 3.35 m kerosene booster with two YF-100 engines and a cone nose: 770 kN in vacuum (about 690 kN at sea level) for 80 s.
parts.role: A liquid booster with two engines.
parts.detail: Long March 5 wears four of these round its 5 m hydrogen core. Each has two YF-100 engines, oxygen-rich staged-combustion kerosene engines that swivel in one plane. The rocket launched China's first Mars mission, Tianwen-1, in July 2020, and the Chang'e 5 Moon sample return.
parts.real: Long March 5 booster (2016–): two YF-100, 2,400 kN sea level / 2,680 kN vacuum, Isp 300 / 335 s, 3.35 m wide

parts.name: Small fin
parts.desc: A small feather for a small arrow.
parts.role: A small fin: a little stability for little mass.
parts.detail: A short fin for a light stack. Fins pull the centre of pressure to the tail; small fins do it gently. Rockets carry them in sets of three or four.
cons: Little stability on a tall stack
parts.real: Redstone fins (four, with air rudders and jet vanes)

parts.name: Fin
parts.desc: Moves the centre of pressure back. Rockets carry them in sets of three or four.
parts.role: A fin: moves the centre of pressure to the tail.
parts.detail: Fins are the feathers on the arrow. Mounted low on the stack they pull the centre of pressure behind the centre of mass, so the ship flies nose-first instead of tumbling. Rockets carry them in sets of three or four.
pros: Pulls the centre of pressure back
parts.real: Saturn IB (eight fins on the S-IB)

parts.name: Large fin
parts.desc: Bigger feathers for a taller arrow.
parts.role: A big fin for a tall stack.
parts.detail: A larger fin for a longer vehicle. More side area low down means more stability in thick air, at the cost of a little mass and drag.
pros: More stability for a tall stack
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC fins (four, one on each engine fairing)

parts.name: Grid fin
parts.desc: A titanium lattice paddle: steers hard in thick air, small to stow.
parts.role: A lattice fin: a lot of steering surface in a small panel.
parts.detail: A grid fin is a box of thin crossed plates: the air flows through the cells instead of around a flat fin. That gives a lot of grip in a small, foldable panel, and it keeps working at supersonic speed. N1 carried four big ones at its base; Falcon 9 flies four titanium ones at the top of its first stage to steer back to the landing pad. Here they clamp low on the tail and add side area like a fin.
pros: Strong steering surface in a small panel
cons: More drag than a flat fin
parts.real: Falcon 9 Block 5 titanium grid fins (about 1.2 × 1.5 m) · N1 Block A lattice fins (four at the base)

parts.name: Engine fairing
parts.desc: A cone-shaped shroud over an outer engine, with room for a fin.
parts.role: Smooths the air over an outboard engine and shields its plumbing.
parts.detail: The four outer F-1 engines of the Saturn V stuck out past the edge of the stage. Each sat under a conical fairing that kept the supersonic air off its turbopump, gimbal and feed lines, and carried one of the four fins. On the Saturn V, one sat over each outer engine.
pros: Shields the outer engines (small reliability bonus)
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC engine fairings (four, each carrying a fin)

parts.name: Aft flap
parts.desc: A big steel flap on a hinge beside the engine bay. Use ×2.
parts.role: Steers the ship like a skydiver's arms when it falls back belly-first.
parts.detail: Starship has four flaps, two forward and two aft. Falling back from space belly-first, it tilts them on motors to steer and stay stable, then flips upright just before landing. On the climb they lie still and add drag and a little stability low on the tail.
pros: Adds stability low on the tail
Steers the real ship on the way down
cons: Needs a heat shield on its windward face
parts.real: Starship aft flaps (2023–): two, beside the engine bay and oxygen tank, hinges sealed in aerocovers; an ablative backing layer was added for flight 6

parts.name: Aft fin
parts.desc: One of four hydraulically driven fins at the base. Use ×4.
parts.role: A moving fin that steadies the climb and steers a falling booster back to its pad.
parts.detail: New Shepard’s booster has four aft fins at its base. Hydraulic actuators swing them even at Mach 4, to steady the climb and to steer the booster back to its landing pad. Higher up, a ring fin and four wedge fins steady the fall, and drag brakes open out of the ring.
pros: Moving fin: steers in thick air
Low on the tail: strong stability
parts.real: New Shepard aft fins (2015–): four, hydraulically actuated through airspeeds up to Mach 4 (Blue Origin); ring fin and wedge fins near the top

parts.name: Landing legs ×4
parts.desc: Four legs. Touch down below 3 m/s.
parts.role: Four landing legs. Touch down below 3 m/s.
parts.detail: Four shock-absorbing legs with pads. They clamp around the engine so the feet reach the ground. A touchdown faster than about 3 m/s, or leaning more than 20 degrees, breaks them.
parts.real: Apollo LM / Falcon 9 legs

parts.name: Heavy landing legs ×4
parts.desc: Longer legs with a wider stance for a tall, heavy ship.
parts.role: Long legs with a wide stance: a tall ship stays upright on a slope.
parts.detail: A tall ship on a slope tips over on short legs. These reach further out and crush more honeycomb on touchdown, so a heavier ship can land a little harder and on rougher ground.
pros: Wide stance for a tall ship
parts.real: Starship / Blue Moon lander legs

parts.name: Folding landing legs ×4
parts.desc: Carbon-fibre legs that ride folded along the tail and swing open to land.
parts.role: Four long, light legs hinged at the base of the thrust structure.
parts.detail: Falcon 9's legs are long carbon-fibre beams with an aluminium honeycomb core. During the climb they lie folded flat against the tail like four strakes; a few seconds before touchdown helium pistons push them open into an 18 m wide stance and lock them. Lighter than fixed legs, and folded they even steady the climb a little. The mechanism has to work every time.
pros: Folded, they act like strakes (more stability)
parts.real: Falcon 9 landing legs: carbon fibre and aluminium honeycomb, about 18 m across when open, helium-piston deployment

parts.name: Landing legs ×6
parts.desc: Six legs folded flush along the tail, opened just before landing on a ship at sea.
parts.role: Six legs for a heavy booster on a rolling deck.
parts.detail: New Glenn's first stage lands at sea on the ship Jacklyn, about 600 km out in the Atlantic. Its legs lie flush against the tail for the climb and swing out just before touchdown; six legs spread the weight of a 7 m booster on a moving deck. The first landing worked on the second flight, on 13 November 2025.
pros: Six legs: a wide, steady stance
parts.real: New Glenn GS1 landing legs (2025–): six hydraulic legs, folded flush on the climb and deployed before landing

parts.name: Booster landing gear ×4
parts.desc: Four short legs that swing down just before touchdown.
parts.role: Light legs for a short booster landing on a flat pad.
parts.detail: New Shepard's booster falls back tail-first, opens its drag brakes, relights its engine low over the ground and settles on four legs that swing down just before touchdown. Nearly all of it flies again: one booster has flown 17 times.
parts.real: New Shepard landing gear (2015–): four legs deployed before landing; booster NS4 flew 17 times

parts.name: Hydraulic engine gimbal
parts.desc: Hydraulic rams swivel the engine to steer during the burn.
parts.role: Lets the main engine swivel to steer during a burn.
parts.detail: A gimbal joint at the top of the engine and two hydraulic rams let it tilt a few degrees, so the thrust itself steers the ship while it burns. This is how real rockets fly straight without big fins. The F-1 and Merlin even use their own pressurised kerosene as the hydraulic fluid.
pros: Steers with the main engine (reliability bonus +0.8 %)
cons: Only works while the engine burns
parts.real: RS-27A and F-1 hydraulic gimbal actuators (the F-1's ran on RP-1 from its own pump)

parts.name: Electric gimbal actuators
parts.desc: Battery-powered screw jacks swivel the engine: no fluid, no leaks.
parts.role: Swivels the engine with electric motors and ball screws instead of hydraulics.
parts.detail: Each actuator is an electric motor turning a ball screw that pushes and pulls the engine. There is no oil, no pump and nothing to leak, and the computer can command it to a fraction of a millimetre. The price is a heavy battery and high-current wiring. Vega and Ariane 6 steer their solid motors this way.
parts.real: Vega P80 and Ariane 6 P120C electro-mechanical TVC actuators

parts.name: Vernier thrusters
parts.desc: Four small swivelling chambers around the main engine do the steering.
parts.role: Steers with small extra engines instead of swivelling the big one.
parts.detail: Instead of moving the main engine, four small rocket chambers on swivel mounts around it push the tail left, right, up or down. The main engine can then be bolted rigidly. The Soyuz core carries four verniers and each booster two; the early Atlas had two. More plumbing, but the main engine stays simple.
pros: Fine control late in the burn
parts.real: Soyuz RD-108A (four verniers) and RD-107A (two) · Atlas LR101 verniers

parts.name: Jet vanes ×4
parts.desc: Four graphite paddles in the exhaust deflect it to steer. Old and cheap.
parts.role: Steers by dipping four heat-proof paddles into the exhaust jet.
parts.detail: The oldest way to steer a rocket: four graphite vanes sit right in the exhaust below the nozzle and tilt like rudders in a river of fire. The V-2 and the Redstone that launched Alan Shepard flew this way. Cheap and simple, but the vanes slowly burn away, and in reality they cost a percent or two of thrust.
cons: The vanes erode in the jet
Only steers while the engine burns
parts.real: V-2 and Redstone graphite jet vanes (four in the exhaust)

parts.name: Landing airbags
parts.desc: Bounce instead of landing. Pathfinder did it; a heavy ship cannot.
parts.role: A cocoon of airbags: the ship bounces to a stop instead of landing on legs.
parts.detail: Pathfinder and the Mars rovers hit the ground inside a ball of airbags and bounced for a kilometre. It works for a light lander and is cheaper than legs, but a crewed ship is heavy and the crew will not enjoy the bounces: reliability 97.5 %.
parts.real: Mars Pathfinder / MER airbags
